title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: Money and Dust—The Novel's Moral Arithmetic

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, unhurried look at one of the great novels of the nineteenth century.
Our Mutual Friend was Charles Dickens's last completed novel, published in 1865, and it is in many ways his most ambitious and unsettling.
It opens with a body pulled from the Thames and a fortune built on dust — the refuse and ash of a city that throws nothing away.
From that first image, the novel asks a question it never stops asking: what is money, and what does it do to everyone it touches?
Joining me today to unpack this extraordinary book are three guests who bring very different lenses to the material.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — he is not interested in letting institutions off the hook.
He will keep us honest about what the novel's money actually means, and who it costs.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian — the person in the room who can tell you exactly what a Victorian dustman's estate looked like in law, and why that matters.
He brings the real world into the conversation — the institutions, the statutes, the people who fell through the cracks.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice behind more classic novel recordings than perhaps anyone alive — comes at the book as a performer.
He hears the rhythms, catches the comedy, and will not let us forget that Dickens was, first and last, a writer who needed to be heard.
We begin where the novel itself begins its moral arithmetic: with the Dust Heaps, the fortune, and the question of what good and evil actually leave behind.
What strikes me first, coming back to this novel, is how precisely Dickens understands the difference between inherited wealth and earned virtue.
The Boffins are, by any conventional Victorian measure, nobody — servants, functionally illiterate in the language of polite society.
And yet Dickens insists that their moral straightness is not incidental — it is the structural argument of the whole book.
There is a passage where the narrator describes how even the hard, wrathful old miser who worked them to the bone could not entirely resist what they were.
And the narrator draws from that a law — almost a cosmic law.
That is Dickens at his most polemical — and most serious.
Evil exhausts itself in the person who commits it. Good outlasts its origin.
That line lands like a sermon — and I mean that as praise.
Dickens knew exactly the effect of that short sentence after all those long qualifying clauses.
You build and build — ten thousand weaknesses, ten thousand vanities — and then you get four words: but Good, never.
It is a preacher's trick. Dickens learned it from the King James Bible and spent a career perfecting it.
But what I find equally thrilling is that the novel immediately puts that virtue under extraordinary financial pressure.
The moment the Boffins inherit, the world descends on them — and I mean descends, like a flock of very well-dressed birds of prey.
And that descent is documented with a precision that is, I think, still underappreciated as social record.
The Victorian charitable sector was, in reality, exactly as Dickens portrays it: lavish in administrative expenditure, aggressive in its pursuit of wealthy donors.
The narrator's inventory of solicitations is comic, but the underlying mechanism is real.
The passage describes what the Secretary reads, and the narrator breaks into this gleeful satirical catalogue.
There is the Duke of Linseed, for instance, pressing Boffin to become a Steward of a charity.
The physical description of the letter does the work — pompous, sealed with the coronet, utterly impersonal.
And then Dickens delivers the detail that kills it: lithographed by the hundred, with the address filled in quite another hand.
What I want to press on is the structural irony here.
Charity, in this novel, is not a mechanism for redistribution. It is a mechanism for extraction.
Money flows upward — from the newly enriched Boffin toward the aristocracy and the institutions the aristocracy controls.
And then there are the individual beggars — the passage is even more ruthless about them.
Dickens gives us this devastating line about the documents they enclose — their proofs of misery.
That comparison is savage and true — and it cuts in two directions at once.
The beggars are deluded about the weight of their evidence, yes — but the system that requires such evidence from desperate people is itself the indictment.
The comedy of that catalogue is genuinely dazzling — the inspired beggars sitting by a fragment of candle, the nobly independent beggars who wouldn't dream of accepting money, except as a loan.
And the beggars of punctual business habits — who will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one precisely, unless a postal order arrives.
Dickens is doing multiple things at once: the comic types are hilarious, and the desperation underneath is absolutely genuine.
That is the particular genius of this novel — the joke and the wound occupy the same sentence.
And the fortune that triggers all of this descends from a man who, by his own account, never made a friend in his life.
There is a document — a will found by Wegg and Venus late in the novel — that puts the whole question of the Harmon estate with remarkable bluntness.
No sentiment. No legacy. Just the Crown — the state — inheriting by default.
It tells you something important about what old Harmon's fortune actually was: not the product of affection or relationship, but of isolation and extraction.
The dust heaps are the perfect metaphor precisely because dust is what accumulates when nothing living is happening.
Dust as absence — that is a remarkable way to put it, and it sets up everything the novel will do with money from here on.
We have the moral law — good never dies — and we have the system that tests it at every turn: the charities, the letters, the locked wills.
In our next segment, we turn to the river — the other great force in this novel — and what it takes and what it gives back.

segments.title: Bella's Reckoning: From Mercenary to Human

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
Today we're turning to one of the novel's most carefully constructed arcs — Bella Wilfer's transformation from self-declared mercenary to something far more complicated and human.
And bound up with Bella is the extraordinary confession at the heart of Book Two — John Harmon's account of why he chose to remain dead.
With me today are three guests who I think will pull this in productively different directions.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads Dickens as a diagnostician of class power — and who will not let the novel's sentimentality pass without scrutiny.
Prof. James Blackstone brings the legal and social history — what these institutions actually were, what it meant to inherit a fortune built on dust mounds and dead men's wills.

And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, the voice of more Dickens audiobooks than is perhaps entirely healthy — brings the performer's ear to everything Dickens wrote to be heard rather than merely read.
Let's begin with John Harmon's confession — because before we can talk about Bella's transformation, we need to understand the mechanism designed to produce it.
What strikes me first — as a performer — is how Dickens constructs Harmon's confession as a man literally cross-examining himself.
He's in the witness box and the dock simultaneously.
Listen to the rhythm when he catalogues his own anxieties on returning to England:

'I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife, mistrustful of my father's intention in thrusting that marriage on me, mistrustful that I was already growing avaricious.'
That triple repetition of 'shrinking' and 'mistrustful' — it's practically incantatory.
Dickens is writing anxiety as a speech impediment — the mind stuttering under its own weight.
And then — gloriously — he wraps up with: 'Is that so? That is exactly so.'
Oliver's right that it's rhetorically astonishing — but I want to press on what Harmon is actually confessing to.
He devises a scheme — with a man called Radfoot — to observe Bella without her knowledge, dress as common sailors, infiltrate her neighbourhood.
The novel calls it a 'plot,' and that word is doing a great deal of work.
Harmon describes it plainly:
'the plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses, and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way.'
A man with enormous inherited wealth disguises himself as a poor sailor in order to surveil the woman he's been assigned to marry.
The power asymmetry is staggering, and the novel never quite forces Harmon to reckon with it.

I'd add a dimension to Daniel's point about power — because in 1865, the legal reality of marriage and inheritance made this surveillance not merely a romantic eccentricity but a rational economic calculation.
A man of Harmon's fortune, married under a testamentary compulsion to a woman he'd never met, would have virtually no recourse once the marriage was made.
Harmon says himself that his father's wealth had brought about 'nothing but wretchedness' — and he feared perpetuating exactly that.
'The dread of our being forced on one another, and perpetuating the fate that seemed to have fallen on my father's riches — the fate that they should lead to nothing but evil.'
That's not simply romantic anxiety — that is a man reasoning carefully about inherited corruption.
Whether his method of testing Bella was ethical is another question entirely — and Daniel is right to name the asymmetry.
I don't entirely disagree with either of you — but I think we risk flattening what is also a genuinely tragicomic situation.
Here is a man who is, by legal definition, dead — who must convince himself of his own remembered facts like a barrister refreshing his brief.
'I have all these facts right? Yes. They are all accurately right.'
There's something almost Beckettian about that — a man insisting to himself that he exists.
Dickens was writing this sixty years before Beckett, and he found the same abyss by a completely different road.
That abyss is worth sitting with for a moment — because the novel counterpoints Harmon's existential vertigo with something almost defiantly cosy in the Boffins.
Daniel, I wonder if you'd like to take up the Boffins — because Dickens does something rather sly with their virtue and their social failure.
The Boffins are Dickens's great proof that goodness and fashionability are structurally incompatible in this novel's world.
When Mr Boffin tells his wife he loves her, Dickens renders it as social doom.
'Yes; and it's pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin, and it's been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a year!'
And then, immediately: 'It was ruin to Mrs Boffin's aspirations, but, having so spoken, they sat side by side, a hopelessly Unfashionable pair.'
That capital U on 'Unfashionable' is Dickens's verdict on the whole system of social aspiration.
Warmth, fidelity, pleasure in one another's company — these are, by the logic of fashionable society, disqualifying.
And the irony, historically, is that the newly wealthy — the Boffins' position in the 1860s — were doing exactly what Dickens satirises: purchasing titles of association, patronages, civic prestige.
Which is why Mr Boffin's outburst about charity lists is so precisely aimed.

'Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses — what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!'
The proliferation of titles is Dickens's image of philanthropy as vanity publishing — everyone a patron, no one actually helping anyone.
And 'up to his neck' is magnificent — Rokesmith drowning not in need but in self-congratulation.
That speech is an absolute gift to read aloud — the repetition builds like a comic aria and then Boffin punctures it with 'What the deuce is it all about?'
But notice who's present when Boffin delivers it: Bella and Rokesmith.
Dickens is staging Bella's moral education as a series of object lessons — and Boffin is the most unexpected teacher imaginable.
A Golden Dustman railing against fake charity while surrounded by people testing and being tested — it's almost diagrammatic.
And yet — I want to hold this tension — the 'testing' of Bella never quite escapes the logic it claims to critique.
Harmon says the danger he survived gave him the idea of 'proving Bella' — that verb is telling.
'the thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella.'
You prove metal by subjecting it to heat — you prove a woman by subjecting her to poverty and proximity to a wealthy man she doesn't know is her future husband.
The novel wants us to find this romantic — and Dickens is too great a writer for it to be entirely dishonest — but the power structure underneath is unchanged.
I think that's exactly right, and it matters for how we read Bella's transformation — because the novel presents it as entirely internal and moral, when it is also materially conditioned.
Bella changes in proximity to the Boffins' wealth and, later, in the structured genteel poverty of life with Rokesmith.
She is never actually poor — she is performing poverty under supervision, much as Harmon performed being a common sailor under the cover of his own plan.
The symmetry is uncomfortable, and I suspect Dickens knew it.
There's one more figure in this segment we haven't touched — and he offers perhaps the darkest counterpoint to all this talk of transformation and moral growth.
Oliver — Bradley Headstone.
Headstone is where the novel goes cold and terrifying — and Dickens describes his inner state with a precision that still unsettles.
He is cursed — and that's Dickens's word — with something worse than remorse.
'He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently.'
No remorse — but an endless compulsive rehearsal of how it might have been done better.
That is genuinely modern psychology — and it is also the most frightening portrait of a mind in this novel.
Bella changes; Harmon reconstructs himself; the Boffins remain cheerfully, hopelessly decent — and Headstone simply loops, forever.
And what condemns Headstone — I think Dickens is clear on this — is precisely that he has no framework outside himself.
Bella's transformation is enabled by community — the Boffins, Rokesmith, her father.
Headstone has only his own grinding, airless interiority — and the crime that he cannot stop improving in his imagination.
The novel suggests, I think, that character is relational — you cannot become better or worse in isolation.
Relational character — that feels like the right note to hold as we move forward.
Bella can only be proved — to use Harmon's unsettling verb — in relation to others, however manipulated that relation might be.
And Headstone is imprisoned in a relation only with his own crime.
We'll pick up those threads — and a great deal else — in the next part of the episode.

segments.title: The Gentleman in the Shadows: John Harmon's Double Life

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — the programme dedicated to the finest, strangest, and most ambitious novel Dickens ever wrote.
I'm joined today by three voices I trust completely to do this book justice.
Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — and who has no patience for sentimentality that doesn't earn itself.
Prof James Blackstone brings the legal and social historian's eye — the actual institutions, the actual stakes, the actual suffering behind the fiction.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man who has voiced more Dickens than anyone alive — reads the prose the way it was always meant to be heard.
Today's segment sits at the emotional and structural heart of the novel: John Harmon's disguise, his hidden past, and the extraordinary figures of the Boffins.
We begin where the novel begins its real excavation — with Boffin himself recounting what John Harmon's childhood actually looked like.
What strikes me first, every single time, is that Boffin is the great unacknowledged rhetorician of this novel.
He speaks in a vernacular that people condescend to — and then absolutely devastates them with it.
He's recounting to Mortimer Lightwood how he and Mrs Boffin stood up for young John against old Harmon — repeatedly, over years — and got nothing but abuse for it.

"I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet — she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head — and send it spinning across the yard."
And then Dickens gives Boffin the simplest, most lethal pair of sentences in the chapter.
"Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her."
That repetition — the plain verb, repeated, nothing else — is as good a piece of comic-tragic writing as you'll find anywhere in the book.
And what that passage reveals, underneath the comic timing Oliver rightly praises, is a very specific power structure.
Old Harmon holds absolute dominion over his domestic world — he can strike, humiliate, dispossess, all without consequence.
The Boffins are loyal retainers who intercede on behalf of the child and are treated with contempt for it.
That is not an eccentric domestic arrangement — that is the standard Victorian property regime, made visible.
The boy is not loved by his father — he is an heir, a legal instrument, a vessel for the continuation of accumulated capital.

And when Boffin says the poor boy gets no good of the money — that he was made away with at the moment he lifted the cup and saucer to his lips — he is describing what happens when the system finally extends its hand to those it has ground down.
It gives, and it immediately takes back.
Daniel is right about the property regime — and it's worth being precise about what that meant in practice.
Old Harmon's will could, and did, attach conditions to the inheritance — conditions concerning whom the heir must marry.
A child could be disinherited for any reason, or none, and the law would not intervene.
So the violence Oliver describes — the bonnet spinning across the yard, Mrs Boffin struck down — that is not aberration.
That is what unchecked patriarchal authority looks like in a household where property is everything and affection is nothing.
And the novel doesn't leave it as violence and abstraction — it gives us the single most affecting image of what that childhood cost John Harmon.
Boffin's account of the last time he and Mrs Boffin saw the boy — seven years old, about to be shipped abroad — is, I think, one of the most tender passages Dickens ever wrote.
It is — and performing it is one of the great quiet challenges, because the comedy is entirely absent and the prose slows down into something quite different.
Boffin describes the child coming in from the cold, his little scanty box outside in the wind — because old Harmon wouldn't allow a sixpence of coach-money.

"Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks; but seeing the tears come into the child's eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, 'I'd give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!'"
The repetition of 'wide wide world' — Dickens heard that, from some real voice, somewhere.
Nobody invents that phrasing at a desk.
What I want to hold onto in that passage is the specific texture of the child's poverty alongside the coming wealth.
The scanty clothes, the scanty box, no coach-money — this is a wealthy man's son being sent out into the world as if he were a pauper.
Old Harmon's cruelty is not mere eccentricity — it is the systematic withholding of care as a mechanism of control.
And Dickens is precise about what it produces: a child who looks up at the only two kind people in his world with a look that Boffin calls — in agony.
That look haunts Mrs Boffin for years — she wakes at night crying out to shelter the poor child.
This is what the inheritance of great wealth costs — not the inheritor, but the people decent enough to care about him.
And it's worth noting what Mrs Boffin does with that haunting — she transforms it into action.
Once the fortune comes to the Boffins — once the boy is presumed dead — she proposes something quietly extraordinary.
"Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him."
She wants to give the money the moral shape it was always denied — to make it do, for some unknown child, what it never did for John.
That is an act of redemptive imagination that the legal and institutional worlds of this novel are utterly incapable of.
And the irony, of course, is achingly beautiful — because the orphan child the Boffins end up sheltering is, in a sense, John Harmon himself.
He arrives in disguise, under the name Rokesmith — and they take him in.
They don't know who he is, and they give him shelter, purpose, and eventually full restoration — because that is simply who they are.
Mrs Boffin's wish — that wild, impractical wish to run away with the child — is answered by the plot itself.
Which brings us to the moment when the disguise is finally stripped away — and John Harmon names, with absolute clarity, what he owes and to whom.
He is confronting Silas Wegg — the novel's most contemptible parasite — and he draws a direct line between Wegg's presumption and the Boffins' nobility.
"I owe everything I possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness, goodness — there are no words to satisfy me — of Mr and Mrs Boffin."
That parenthetical — there are no words to satisfy me — is Dickens acknowledging, through Harmon, that the moral vocabulary available to the period is simply unequal to describing genuine virtue.
He has to list — disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness, goodness — and then confess the list is still insufficient.
That is not sentimental excess — that is a structural critique of how poverty makes goodness invisible and unspeakable.
And notice the legal precision underneath the emotion.
Harmon tells Wegg that he possesses his father's property — but not through any act of his father's, and not by any right.
Through the munificence of Mr Boffin — who made conditions, who struck a bargain, who chose to give the money back rather than keep it.
Boffin kept only his Mound — the literal rubbish heap that was always his domain — and surrendered the legal fortune.
In a novel obsessed with wills, inheritance, and the law, the most legally significant act is a voluntary renunciation made in private, witnessed only by the people it concerns.
And what makes the final confrontation theatrically irresistible is the sheer contained fury of Harmon's voice.
Dickens gives us 'through his clenched teeth' and 'a very ugly turn indeed on Wegg's cravat' — the violence barely leashed.
The man who has spent the entire novel watching from shadows — silent, secretive, self-effacing — suddenly has his hands on someone's throat.
And what he is furious about is not the money, not the disguise, not even the conspiracy against him.
It is that a mud-worm — his word — dared to rise against a noble soul.
The whole disguise plot, in the end, resolves itself into a defence of the Boffins.
Which returns us — beautifully — to where we began: to a seven-year-old boy looking up from a fireside with a look of agony, and two people who never forgot it.
John Harmon's double life is not merely a plot device — it is the novel's argument that identity, stripped of money and name, resolves into the question of who loved you when you had nothing.
Daniel, James, Oliver — thank you.
We'll return shortly with our next segment.

segments.title: Laughter Against the Machine: Comedy as Social Weapon

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
Today we're asking a question that sounds almost paradoxical: what is Dickens doing when he makes us laugh?
Is comedy in this novel a release valve — or is it something sharper, something that cuts?
To dig into that, I'm joined by three extraordinary readers of this book.
Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — and who will not let comedy off the hook.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what it meant, in Dickens's England, to be poor, to be indebted, to be at someone else's mercy.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, the voice of more classic audiobooks than anyone alive — who hears Dickens the way a musician hears a score.
Oliver, let's start with you — because you live inside these comic passages more than most people ever will.
The thing about Dickens's comedy is that it is never decorative.
It is load-bearing.
Take Silas Wegg — this magnificent, preposterous schemer — laying out his plan to blackmail Boffin with the solemnity of a cabinet minister.
He keeps calling Venus his 'comrade, brother, and partner' — like a revolutionary pamphlet — while plotting something entirely squalid.
And then Dickens delivers this, and I have to read it because nothing I say will do it justice.
'He considered it plain that such price was stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, Halves!'
That one word — 'Halves!' — landing after all that elaborate legal-sounding machinery — is one of the great comic punchlines in the novel.
But notice what the joke is actually built on.
Wegg adopts the full grammar of bourgeois property rights — partnership, contract, price — to conduct what is nakedly extortion.
The comedy comes from the gap between the register and the act — and that gap is precisely the gap that capitalism itself operates in, every day.
And then Dickens goes further — and this is where I think the passage becomes genuinely savage.
'He should be kept in a state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his possessions.'
Wegg uses the word 'slavery' without flinching — and Dickens uses it deliberately.
The comedy doesn't neutralise the horror — it concentrates it.
And there is something historically precise in Wegg's plan that makes it more disturbing than it first appears.
The idea of letting someone else bear the cost of excavation while you surveil the process from the shadows — that is a genuinely sophisticated model of extractive capitalism.
Wegg's scheme isn't a parody of business — it is business, with the polite language stripped away.
And Oliver's point about the rhetoric of 'comrade, brother, and partner' — in Victorian law, partnership brought specific obligations and liabilities.
Wegg is invoking legal solidarity while planning outright theft.
Though one does have to admire the audacity — 'it might be more according to the rights of things to say Two-thirds; it might be more according to the rights of things to say Three-fourths.'
He opens the negotiation with himself.
But comedy in Our Mutual Friend isn't only weaponised against the villains.
Some of the most beautiful comic writing is tender — almost pastoral.
There's a scene — Bella and Rokesmith and old R. Wilfer sharing a modest supper in an office — that is just utterly disarming.
Dickens reaches for a fairy-tale image — listen to this —

'It was, as Bella gaily said, like the supper provided for the three nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous low growlings of the alarming discovery, Somebody's been drinking my milk!'
The joy in that passage is real — the comedy earns the tenderness rather than undercutting it.
And the setting intensifies it — the iron safe of Chicksey, Veneering, and Stobbles staring from the corner.
Dickens calls it 'like the eyes of some dull dragon' — the machinery of commerce literally watching their happiness.
The joke and the critique land together — that is Dickens at his most disciplined.
There's a different kind of comic writing I want to bring in — the portrait of Mrs Sprodgkin and the Milveys.
The narrator tells us she has a sixth sense for knowing when the Reverend Milvey least desires her company — and arrives accordingly.
It's a very precise observation about a very particular kind of parishioner that anyone who has sat through church governance will recognise immediately.
But then Dickens goes somewhere unexpected — this wonderful, absurd sentence about how Mrs Sprodgkin received her gifts.
'She regarded tea and sugar in the light of myrrh and frankincense, and considered bread and butter identical with locusts and wild honey.'
That sentence is a theological joke, a class joke, and a portrait of institutional charity's impossible clients — all at once.
And the narrator's sign-off on that scene is magnificent — 'all of which is here recorded to the honour of that good Christian pair.'
It's affectionate irony — not savage, not dismissive — just the warmth of someone who sees the absurdity and the goodness simultaneously.
Which brings me to what I think is the most purely delightful comic moment I've been assigned — the unmasking of Sloppy.
Wegg has been tormenting — or believes he has been tormenting — this apparently broken-headed, bandaged figure, the 'ever-wakeful dustman.'
And then — I will read it exactly as it stands, because to paraphrase it would be vandalism —
'Somebody else had come in quietly by the folding-doors. Turning his head, Wegg beheld his persecutor, the ever-wakeful dustman, accoutred with fantail hat and velveteen smalls complete.'
'Who, untying his tied-up broken head, revealed a head that was whole, and a face that was Sloppy's.'
The rhythm of that final clause — 'a face that was Sloppy's' — lands like a cymbal crash.
And it's Sloppy — of all people — who gets to unmask the schemer.
Not a magistrate, not a solicitor — the dustman, the orphan, the boy who reads the newspaper aloud and was mocked for it.
Comedy here is restitution — the most marginalised character in the book gets the best joke.
And there is a parallel moment — different in tone, but equally as earned — when Bella kneels beside Boffin and recants everything she thought she knew about him.
She's laughing while she does it — 'with an exultant ringing laugh' — which is important.
The emotion is released through comedy, not instead of it.
The line itself is almost childlike in its syntax — and that is entirely the point.
'Please I don't believe you are a hard-hearted miser at all, and please I don't believe you ever for one single minute were!'
She dismantles an entire false identity with a nursery construction — 'please.'
What strikes me across all these passages is that Dickens's comedy never pretends the world is better than it is.
Wegg's scheme is genuinely predatory; Mrs Sprodgkin's demands are genuinely exhausting; Boffin's performance has genuinely hurt people.
The laughter doesn't redeem the injustice — it illuminates it.
That phrase — the laughter illuminates rather than redeems — feels like a key to the whole novel.
Dickens, writing in what would be his final completed novel, is not offering easy comfort.
The comedy is serious work — and our three guests have made that unmistakably clear today.
Thank you to Daniel Rosen, James Blackstone, and Oliver Trevelyan — and we'll be back with Our Mutual Friend Unpacked very soon.

segments.title: The New Man and the Old Corruption: Boffin's Moral Test

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — and with great pleasure.
I'm your host, and today we're joined by three remarkable readers of this extraordinary book.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every novel as an anatomy of class power — and Our Mutual Friend gives him more to work with than almost anything else in the canon.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows what the institutions in this novel actually were — and what it cost, in pounds and in dignity, to be caught inside them.
And Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has read more Dickens aloud than anyone alive — and who hears things in the prose the rest of us simply miss.
Today's segment is called The New Man and the Old Corruption — and we're looking at what this novel does with suffering, money, class, and the strange comedy of the body.
Let's begin with something that sounds light but is anything but — Sloppy, dressed for company.
Sloppy's entrance in his black suit is one of those passages where Dickens is simply showing off — and he's absolutely right to.
The tailor has been instructed — at Rokesmith's personal direction — to conceal the buttons.
And Sloppy's body simply refuses.
The prose enacts it perfectly — listen to this:
"he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators."
The Argus of Greek myth — the hundred-eyed giant — pressed into service to describe a young man who can't keep his buttons under control.
That is comic genius — and it is also, I think, unexpectedly tender.
Tender, yes — but the comedy has a precise social address.
The suit has been paid for by Mrs Boffin's consideration — that word is deliberate — and it cannot fit, because Sloppy's body has been formed by labour and poverty, not by a life that suits fit.
The tailoring science fails because it is trying to impose respectable form on a body that the system has made otherwise.
What's brilliant is that Dickens doesn't let that be grim — he lets it be glorious.
Sloppy doesn't suffer from his buttons — he blazes with them.
There is something sharply legible here about the costume of respectability in mid-Victorian England.
The black suit was the uniform of the respectable working man, the clerk, the artisan who had arrived — it signalled moral standing as much as social position.
On Sloppy it becomes a beautiful impossibility — and that impossibility is the novel's joke at the expense of the entire system of social legibility.
The hatter contributes a fluted hatband that the narrative tells us the imagination shrank from — the prose itself has opinions about this hat.
The prose does have opinions — very strong ones — and they are delivered with perfect comic timing.
"the imagination shrunk discomfited and the reason revolted" — that is a joke constructed with the precision of a watch.
But I want to turn to something far darker now, because this novel earns its comedy against a landscape of real horror.
That landscape you're pointing toward is the river — and the extraordinary passage where Dickens imagines what the Thames whispers to people like Betty Higden.
Daniel, this is one of the passages assigned to you — what do you make of it?
This is the most savage passage in the book, and it's written in the key of pastoral beauty — which is precisely the point.
Dickens imagines the river speaking — not to the comfortable, but to those driven to the edge of endurance by the Poor Law and the workhouse.
The river offers itself as a Relieving Officer — which was the actual title of the bureaucrat who administered workhouse relief.
And the passage makes the comparison explicit and unflinching:
"I am the Relieving Officer appointed by eternal ordinance to do my work; I am not held in estimation according as I shirk it.
My breast is softer than the pauper-nurse's; death in my arms is peacefuller than among the pauper-wards."
Death is kinder than the institution.
That is Dickens's verdict on the Victorian welfare system — and he delivers it in the voice of a river.
The Relieving Officer comparison is not figurative decoration — it is precise to the point of being almost documentary.
The 1834 Poor Law Amendment Act was designed, deliberately and consciously, to make relief so degrading that only the truly desperate would accept it.
The pauper-nurse was a real figure — an inmate caring for other inmates, frequently drunk, frequently neglectful, because what other arrangement could the system produce?
Dickens knew this from his journalism, from his social work, from observation — and here he turns it into something close to myth.
A river that is more humane than the state — that is a very particular kind of accusation.
When I read that passage aloud, I always pause before the river begins speaking.
Because Dickens tells us something remarkable: Betty Higden cannot quite articulate these thoughts herself.
"It were too much to pretend that Betty Higden made out such thoughts" — the river is not her inner monologue; it is the novel's moral imagination speaking on her behalf.
That distinction matters enormously — it's the narrator intervening, taking up the case, becoming the advocate that the law refuses to be.
There's another kind of suffering in the novel — quieter, but just as corrosive — and that's the slow grinding of debt.
James, you've been thinking about Twemlow's situation — the man who signed his name for a friend and has been paying for it for years.
Twemlow's case is, as the novel drily notes, something he treats as a terrible phenomenon occurring in the course of ages — when in fact it happened every day.
'Giving his name' — that is, acting as guarantor — was a practice that destroyed more respectable men than almost any other financial instrument of the period.
And the novel's description of how he has managed it is worth listening to carefully:
"he had always pinched the full interest out of himself with punctual pinches."
Punctual pinches — the alliteration performs the very thing it describes: small, regular, bodily pain, managed with meticulous discipline.
That is a sentence constructed with both moral seriousness and considerable craft.
And the person squeezing those pinches is, in the background, the shadow of Snigsworth — Twemlow's noble cousin, the Security in the Mist.
The aristocratic connection is what makes Twemlow creditworthy to money-lenders — and yet the aristocratic income is fixed, limited, insufficient.
He is respectable enough to be exploited, but not powerful enough to be protected.
And the instrument of that exploitation is Fledgeby — who owns Riah's firm and uses Riah as his mask of antisemitic plausible deniability.
It is a very precise diagram of how financial cruelty operates through intermediaries — and it is as modern as this morning.
I love that Twemlow tells Fledgeby all of this expecting to be astonished at — as the novel puts it — 'a terrible phenomenon occurring in the course of ages.'
And Fledgeby — who arranged the whole thing — nods along with counterfeit sympathy.
The comedy there is pitch-black — and Dickens holds it in perfect tension with the genuine pathos of this mild, bewildered old man.
From debt to sacrifice — and to one of the novel's most quietly devastating declarations of love.
Daniel, Lizzie Hexam's speech about her love for Eugene — what do you make of it as a statement of what the novel values?
Lizzie's speech is one of the places where Dickens is most radical — and most in tension with himself.
She explicitly refuses the fantasy of marriage across the class divide — she says she has never dreamed of it, and words, she says, could not be stronger than that.
And yet what she offers instead is this:
"I love him so much, and so dearly, that when I sometimes think my life may be but a weary one, I am proud of it and glad of it.
I am proud and glad to suffer something for him, even though it is of no service to him, and he will never know of it or care for it."
She is taking the class system's verdict on her life — weary, unrewarded, invisible — and converting it into a form of spiritual pride.
That is either deeply conservative or quietly subversive — I have never quite settled which.
I think it is both at once — and that is precisely why it is so affecting when you read it aloud.
The rhythm of that sentence — proud and glad, proud and glad to suffer — has a pulse to it.
It doesn't read like resignation — it reads like something fierce, something chosen.
Whether Dickens intended the critique or the consolation — he wrote something that contains both, and the performer's job is not to resolve that ambiguity.
There is a historical dimension here that sharpens the tension Daniel is describing.
A woman of Lizzie's class and background in the 1860s had almost no available framework for expressing love that crossed a class boundary — other than sacrifice.
The vocabulary of romantic equality simply didn't exist for her — and Dickens knows it.
What she says is the most she can say — and the novel's tragedy is that even that most is more than the world will hear.
And the novel's final test of whether love and justice can coexist comes in a single, extraordinary sentence from Eugene Wrayburn's sickbed.
Daniel — Eugene asks Mortimer for one thing.
He asks for justice to be withheld.
He has been beaten nearly to death — and his one instruction to his oldest friend is:
"I trust to you that the perpetrator is never brought to justice."
Because bringing the perpetrator to justice would expose Lizzie — drag her name through the courts, into the newspapers, ruin the reputation that is her only remaining asset.
So Eugene, for perhaps the first time in his idle, careless life, places someone else's welfare absolutely above his own.
And the instrument of that grace is a refusal of the law.
It is one of the most compressed moments in all of Dickens.
Eugene has spent the entire novel being witty, elusive, deliberately inconclusive about everything — including his intentions toward Lizzie.
And here, on what may be his deathbed, he becomes completely clear — in eleven words.
That is the kind of sentence you can only write when you know exactly what your character is.
The legal dimension of this moment is worth pausing on.
Mortimer Lightwood is a solicitor — a man of the law, professionally obligated to its processes.
Eugene is asking him to betray that professional identity in the name of something the law cannot recognise — which is Lizzie's dignity.
And Mortimer agrees — without hesitation, as far as we can tell.
Which is Dickens saying, quietly but unmistakably, that friendship and love are more binding than the law.
From Sloppy's buttons to Lizzie's pride to Eugene's eleven words — this novel finds the moral measure of its characters in the smallest, most precisely written moments.
Daniel, James, Oliver — this has been a rich and, I think, genuinely illuminating conversation.
We'll be back with more of Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — and more of the novel that keeps rewarding attention.

segments.title: Reading the Real: Dickens's Narrative Mirrors

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart — carefully, lovingly, and without mercy.
I'm your host, and today we're looking at something that runs through this book like a current: the way Dickens uses his narrative to hold up a mirror — and what stares back is rarely comfortable.
With me today are three people whose company I'd want at any table — literary or otherwise.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — and who has a gift for finding the radical impulse hiding inside the respectable Victorian sentence.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who can tell you exactly what the institutions in this novel actually did — and what it cost the people trapped inside them.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice behind more classic audiobooks than any living person — brings the performer's ear: he hears what Dickens wrote for the voice, not just the page.
Let's begin with accusation — one of the most charged moments of theatrical false testimony in the novel, when Riderhood denounces Gaffer Hexam for the Harmon murder.
What I love about this scene — and love is absolutely the right word — is that Riderhood performs the accusation like a man who has rehearsed it before a mirror.
He even handles the drowned cap — turns it over, brushes it — as if the props must be in place before the speech can begin.
And then he delivers this extraordinary formal declaration — listen to the legal rhythm of it:

"I give information that the man that done the Harmon Murder is Gaffer Hexam, the man that found the body. The hand of Jesse Hexam, commonly called Gaffer on the river and along shore, is the hand that done that deed. His hand and no other."
"His hand and no other" — that's not a man speaking, that's a man quoting himself, already hearing his own words read back in a courtroom.
Oliver is right about the performance — but let's be clear about what's being performed and for whom.
Riderhood is a man with no property, no status, no social legibility whatsoever — except in this moment, when he possesses information.
He has found the one currency the system will briefly accept from someone like him: accusation directed upward — or at least sideways — within his own class.
That triple repetition — the hand, the hand, his hand and no other — is Riderhood mimicking the cadences of legal authority because that is the only authority that will register him at all.
And the tragedy — or the irony, depending on where you're standing — is that he's lying, and the system will reward him for it anyway.
The procedural mimicry is worth dwelling on, because Riderhood isn't simply inventing this language — he's absorbed it.
In the 1860s, an informer's testimony — particularly in a murder case — carried genuine legal weight if delivered in the right form, in front of the right authority.
The phrase 'let me be took down' — 'took down again,' he says — means he wants his words recorded, made official, transformed into written evidence.
What Dickens captures with almost anthropological precision is the way legal ritual colonises the speech of those it most routinely crushes.
Riderhood doesn't speak the law — he ventriloquises it — and he knows, instinctively, that only in that borrowed voice will he be heard.
James, that word 'ventriloquises' is exactly it — and it makes me think how different the narrative mirror operates when we move from Riderhood to Lizzie Hexam.
Because there's a passage — Eugene and Lizzie — where Dickens does something I find genuinely extraordinary: he gets inside her self-accusation with a tenderness that is almost unbearable.
She's just witnessed a rare moment of apparent sincerity from Eugene — a man who wears carelessness like a second skin — and it undoes her completely.
The narrator gives us her interior voice in this devastating free indirect form:

"She thought, had she, so far below him and so different, rejected this disinterestedness, because of some vain misgiving that he sought her out, or heeded any personal attractions that he might descry in her?"
She's accusing herself of vanity — of daring to think she might be desirable to him — and collapsing under the weight of the accusation she herself has constructed.
This is where Dickens is most radical and least aware of it, I think.
The novel can see, with perfect clarity, that Lizzie has internalised class shame so deeply that she punishes herself for the crime of being noticed by her social superior.
The phrase 'sinking before her own eyes as she suspected herself' — that is ideology at work on a human soul.
She has become the instrument of her own oppression, and the narrator sees it — describes it — with compassion but without naming the structure that produced it.
The mirror is held up, but Dickens doesn't quite say what it's reflecting.
I'd push back on that slightly — not on the diagnosis but on the framing of what the novel 'names.'
The passage describes Lizzie as 'pure of heart and purpose' — and in context, that phrase carries a very precise social charge.

'Pure' in the Victorian register is a word that does a great deal of unacknowledged work — it's simultaneously a moral compliment and a class marker, distinguishing Lizzie from the women Eugene has presumably encountered at his own social level.
So the novel is naming the structure — obliquely, in the vocabulary available to it — and what it names cuts sharper than we sometimes credit.
There's a passage I want to bring in here that works differently — not on a human face but on the landscape itself — which is where I think Dickens's narrative mirror gets genuinely cosmic.
A train crossing the Thames — and Dickens turns it into something almost terrifying in its modernity.
James, this is very much your territory — but let me read the passage first, because the prose deserves to be heard before it's explained.

"The train rattled among the house-tops, and among the ragged sides of houses torn down to make way for it, and over the swarming streets, and under the fruitful earth, until it shot across the river: bursting over the quiet surface like a bomb-shell, and gone again as if it had exploded in the rush of smoke and steam and glare."
'Bursting over the quiet surface like a bomb-shell' — the Victorian railway as an act of violence on the world it traverses.
And then — and this is the stroke of genius — the simile shifts from bomb-shell to rocket, and from industrial time to Father Time himself.
What strikes me most about that passage — and Oliver, you're right to hear it before analysing it — is the word 'ragged.'
'The ragged sides of houses torn down to make way for it' — this is the literal historical record of railway construction in London.

The railways didn't acquire land from wealthy neighbourhoods if they could possibly avoid it — they drove their lines through the courts and alleys where the poor lived, demolishing tens of thousands of homes.

Dickens catches this in passing — 'torn down to make way for it' — and then the narrative moves on, exactly as the train does: without pausing, without sentiment, indifferent to what it has just described.
The prose form enacts the moral condition of the thing it describes — and that is a very sophisticated narrative mirror indeed.
And then it arrives at Father Time — 'going straight to its end, as Father Time goes to his' — which is where the passage becomes almost metaphysically unsettling.
Because what Dickens is doing there is placing industrial capital and cosmic time in the same grammatical position — equivalent, parallel, equally indifferent to human life.
And from there I want to make a direct line to Bradley Headstone — because the novel's most harrowing image of a man being consumed from within is described in almost identical terms.

Dickens writes of Bradley sitting all night before the fire — rigid, aging, whitening — and the prose describes the process in the passive voice, as if what is happening to him is as impersonal as geological time:

"Rigid before the fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more haggard, its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair degenerating."
'Degenerating' — not fading, not greying, not aging — degenerating.
The word carries a Victorian charge: social degeneration, moral degeneration, the undoing of everything the self-made man was supposed to achieve by discipline and denial.
That passage frightens me every time, and I've read it aloud more than once.
'A charmed flame that was turning him old' — it's as though Dickens has borrowed the logic of a fairy tale and placed it inside a psychological study.
Bradley is both victim of an enchantment and agent of his own destruction — and the fire doesn't care which.
It just burns.
Daniel, your point about the passive voice is the key to the whole passage — 'being overspread with ashes,' 'his hair degenerating.'
Bradley Headstone is the novel's great example of the self-improving working man who has climbed every rung the system offered him — and what the system has made of him is a man capable of murder.
When the system's disciplines finally break in him, the dissolution takes the form of the very process that built him: rigid posture, rigid will, rigid control — all turning to ash.
The mirror here reflects back not an individual failing but a systemic promise reneged upon — and that's the most damning image in the novel.

The bomb-shell crossing the river, Bradley turning to ash before a charmed fire, Lizzie sinking before her own eyes, Riderhood intoning his borrowed legal formula — these are very different scenes, but as a group they show us what Dickens's narrative mirror is actually doing.
It isn't reflecting a world so much as exposing the forces — of time, of class, of law, of self-deception — that the world would rather not see named.
We'll be back after a short break to look at how the novel's comic characters carry some of this same weight — differently, and perhaps more dangerously.

segments.title: Closing: Our Mutual Friend—What Remains After the Dust Settles

utterances.text: We've spent this episode moving through the depths and shallows of Our Mutual Friend — the dust mounds, the river, the drawing rooms, the disguises.
Now, at the close, I want to ask each of you: what remains?
What does this novel leave behind — as impression, as argument, as achievement?
Oliver, let's begin with you — because you live inside these books more intimately than most.
What remains is the voice — that extraordinary, restless, comic-and-tragic voice that never lets you settle.
And what I keep coming back to, at the end, is Eugene Wrayburn — specifically that passage where he describes his father's arrangements for all his children.
It's done in that glorious throwaway style — as if Eugene is barely bothering to be devastating.
Listen to this — Dickens has him say, with perfect comic timing:
"When my second brother was going to be born by-and-by, 'this,' says M. R. F., 'is a little pillar of the church.' Was born, and became a pillar of the church; a very shaky one."
A very shaky one. Three words. The whole English class system skewered in three words.
That's what remains for me — the wit that conceals, and then quietly detonates, the argument.
The wit is real — and it's doing serious institutional work, which is what strikes me about that same passage.
M. R. F. — the Most Respected Father — doesn't consult his children; he pre-assigns them to roles in the social apparatus before they are even born.
The church, the navy, the bar — these are not callings, they are slots in a machinery that grinds regardless of who's inside it.
And the quietly horrifying detail is that it mostly works — except it doesn't, quite.
Pillars that shake, circumnavigators who haven't circumnavigated — the system is simultaneously all-powerful and faintly absurd.
That tension — between the crushing weight of inherited structures and the human muddle that undermines them — is something Dickens never lets go of.
James is right that the machinery runs — but I want to push on what powers it.
What powers it, in this novel above all, is money — and specifically the way money corrupts the very relationships it claims to reward.
The passage about old John Harmon and the Boffins crystallises this with brutal precision.
The old miser raged at them, reviled them — and still he had to write their names in his will.
Because, Dickens tells us, the old man had perceived something that all his gold couldn't change.
"He had perceived the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt."
Powerlessness. That word does extraordinary work.
This is the one thing capital cannot do — it cannot manufacture integrity.
Dickens knew that was a radical thing to show — and he showed it through a miser's grudging defeat.
And the extraordinary thing is that Dickens embeds that same logic inside the love plot.
John Harmon — as Rokesmith — is living proof of the point Daniel just made.
His whole disguise turns on the question: can love be bought, or does wealth only contaminate it?
Dickens lays out Harmon's impossible dilemma with an almost legal precision.
"Was it for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?"
Buying her or punishing her — the inheritance makes both outcomes equally dishonourable.
The only escape is the disguise — and the disguise is, itself, a kind of poverty voluntarily chosen.
Poverty voluntarily chosen — that phrase lands hard, because there is so much involuntary poverty running through this book.
I keep thinking about the passage where Lizzie describes the child Jenny — surrounded, from her cradle, by drunkenness and degradation.
Lizzie says, quietly, of this small ruined life:
"This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle — if she ever had one, Charley."
If she ever had one.
That parenthetical doubt — about whether the child ever even possessed the most basic symbol of infancy — is among the most devastating things in the novel.
And it's delivered not in outrage, but in a passing clause — because for Lizzie, this is simply the texture of the world she inhabits.
That is the novel's most honest moment, I think — honesty earned by restraint rather than rhetoric.
Dickens is often accused of sentimentality — and sometimes the charge sticks.
But in his best passages, suffering is registered without being aestheticised — it is simply allowed to be what it is.
What remains, for me, after this novel, is the sense that its radicalism lies precisely there — in the refusal to look away from what poverty actually produces.
Not sentiment. Witness.
Witness — yes. And genius in the execution, which is what makes it bearable to sit with.
The comedy and the suffering coexist in this book the way they coexist in life — not alternating, but simultaneous.
That is the hardest thing to do in fiction, and Dickens does it more consistently here than almost anywhere else in his work.
A shaky pillar of the church — and a cradle that may never have existed.
Both true. Both Dickens. Both this novel.
Witness, genius, and the simultaneous — I can't think of a better set of coordinates for where Our Mutual Friend lives.
My thanks to Daniel Rosen, James Blackstone, and Oliver Trevelyan — three guides I would trust across any river this novel cares to throw at us.
Our Mutual Friend: still, after all this time, churning up the sediment — and finding gold.

c9:p29.text:
These two ignorant and unpolished people had guided themselves so far on
      in their journey of life, by a religious sense of duty and desire to do
      right. Ten thousand weaknesses and absurdities might have been detected in
      the breasts of both; ten thousand vanities additional, possibly, in the
      breast of the woman. But the hard wrathful and sordid nature that had
      wrung as much work out of them as could be got in their best days, for as
      little money as could be paid to hurry on their worst, had never been so
      warped but that it knew their moral straightness and respected it. In its
      own despite, in a constant conflict with itself and them, it had done so.
      And this is the eternal law. For, Evil often stops short at itself and
      dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.
c9:p29.summary: Dickens reflects that the Boffins, though ignorant and unpolished, have been guided by genuine religious duty and moral righteousness that even hardened souls cannot entirely resist.
c9:p29.best_quote: For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.

c17:p4.text:
But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.
c17:p4.summary: The Secretary describes the flood of charitable solicitations and scheme proposals that inundate the Boffins, including a satirical example of a duke's letter requesting Boffin become a Steward of a charity for a three-guinea fee.
c17:p4.best_quote: Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.
c17:p5.best_quote: they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf

c40:p31.text:
‘Exactly so, sir!’ returned Wegg, blandly and buoyantly. ‘I see I take you
      with me! Hear, hear, hear! Resolved, as your discriminating good sense

      that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing
      the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently. In the defensive
      declarations and pretended confessions of murderers, the pursuing shadow
      of this torture may be traced through every lie they tell. If I had done
      it as alleged, is it conceivable that I would have made this and this
      mistake? If I had done it as alleged, should I have left that unguarded
      place which that false and wicked witness against me so infamously deposed
      to? The state of that wretch who continually finds the weak spots in his
      own crime, and strives to strengthen them when it is unchangeable, is a
      state that aggravates the offence by doing the deed a thousand times
      instead of once; but it is a state, too, that tauntingly visits the
      offence upon a sullen unrepentant nature with its heaviest punishment
      every time.

‘The last time me and Mrs Boffin saw the poor boy,’ said Mr Boffin,
      warming (as fat usually does) with a tendency to melt, ‘he was a child of
      seven year old. For when he came back to make intercession for his sister,
      me and Mrs Boffin were away overlooking a country contract which was to be
      sifted before carted, and he was come and gone in a single hour. I say he
      was a child of seven year old. He was going away, all alone and forlorn,
      to that foreign school, and he come into our place, situate up the yard of
      the present Bower, to have a warm at our fire. There was his little scanty
      travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in
      the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the
      steamboat, as the old man wouldn’t hear of allowing a sixpence
      coach-money. Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a
      full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two
      open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks; but seeing the tears come
      into the child’s eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him
      round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, “I’d
      give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!” I don’t say but
      what it cut me, and but what it at the same time heightened my feelings of
      admiration for Mrs Boffin. The poor child clings to her for awhile, as she
      clings to him, and then, when the old man calls, he says “I must go! God
      bless you!” and for a moment rests his heart against her bosom, and looks
      up at both of us, as if it was in pain—in agony. Such a look! I went
      aboard with him (I gave him first what little treat I thought he’d like),
      and I left him when he had fallen asleep in his berth, and I came back to
      Mrs Boffin. But tell her what I would of how I had left him, it all went
      for nothing, for, according to her thoughts, he never changed that look
      that he had looked up at us two. But it did one piece of good. Mrs Boffin
      and me had no child of our own, and had sometimes wished that how we had
      one. But not now. “We might both of us die,” says Mrs Boffin, “and other
      eyes might see that lonely look in our child.” So of a night, when it was
      very cold, or when the wind roared, or the rain dripped heavy, she would
      wake sobbing, and call out in a fluster, “Don’t you see the poor child’s
      face? O shelter the poor child!”—till in course of years it gently
      wore out, as many things do.’

‘Now, scoundrel,’ he pursued, ‘I am going to finish. You supposed me just

      goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin. And

c40:p72.text:
On this head, Silas Wegg had much to say. Silas had to say That, he would
      beg to remind his comrade, brother, and partner, of the impressive
      passages they had read that evening; of the evident parallel in Mr
      Boffin’s mind between them and the late owner of the Bower, and the
      present circumstances of the Bower; of the bottle; and of the box. That,
      the fortunes of his brother and comrade, and of himself were evidently
      made, inasmuch as they had but to put their price upon this document, and
      get that price from the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour: who
      now appeared to be less of a minion and more of a worm than had been
      previously supposed. That, he considered it plain that such price was
      stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, ‘Halves!’
      That, the question then arose when ‘Halves!’ should be called. That, here
      he had a plan of action to recommend, with a conditional clause. That, the
      plan of action was that they should lie by with patience; that, they
      should allow the Mounds to be gradually levelled and cleared away, while
      retaining to themselves their present opportunity of watching the process—which
      would be, he conceived, to put the trouble and cost of daily digging and
      delving upon somebody else, while they might nightly turn such complete
      disturbance of the dust to the account of their own private investigations—and
      that, when the Mounds were gone, and they had worked those chances for
      their own joint benefit solely, they should then, and not before, explode
      on the minion and worm. But here came the conditional clause, and to this
      he entreated the special attention of his comrade, brother, and partner.
      It was not to be borne that the minion and worm should carry off any of
      that property which was now to be regarded as their own property. When he,
      Mr Wegg, had seen the minion surreptitiously making off with that bottle,
      and its precious contents unknown, he had looked upon him in the light of
      a mere robber, and, as such, would have despoiled him of his ill-gotten
      gain, but for the judicious interference of his comrade, brother, and
      partner. Therefore, the conditional clause he proposed was, that, if the
      minion should return in his late sneaking manner, and if, being closely
      watched, he should be found to possess himself of anything, no matter
      what, the sharp sword impending over his head should be instantly shown
      him, he should be strictly examined as to what he knew or suspected,
      should be severely handled by them his masters, and should be kept in a
      state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should
      see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his
      possessions. If, said Mr Wegg by way of peroration, he had erred in saying
      only ‘Halves!’ he trusted to his comrade, brother, and partner not to
      hesitate to set him right, and to reprove his weakness. It might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Two-thirds; it might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Three-fourths. On those points
      he was ever open to correction.

If Boffin is caught secretly removing anything, they will interrogate and enslave him morally until he pays for his freedom.

This very exacting member of the fold appeared to be endowed with a sixth
      sense, in regard of knowing when the Reverend Frank Milvey least desired
      her company, and with promptitude appearing in his little hall.

      announced as in faithful attendance below, desiring counsel on a spiritual
      matter. The points on which Mrs Sprodgkin sought elucidation being seldom
      of a pressing nature (as Who begat Whom, or some information concerning
      the Amorites), Mrs Milvey on this special occasion resorted to the device
      of buying her off with a present of tea and sugar, and a loaf and butter.
      These gifts Mrs Sprodgkin accepted, but still insisted on dutifully
      remaining in the hall, to curtsey to the Reverend Frank as he came forth.

      are!’ involved himself in a discursive address from Mrs Sprodgkin,
      revolving around the result that she regarded tea and sugar in the light
      of myrrh and frankincense, and considered bread and butter identical with
      locusts and wild honey. Having communicated this edifying piece of
      information, Mrs Sprodgkin was left still unadjourned in the hall, and Mr
      and Mrs Milvey hurried in a heated condition to the railway station. All
      of which is here recorded to the honour of that good Christian pair,
      representatives of hundreds of other good Christian pairs as conscientious
      and as useful, who merge the smallness of their work in its greatness, and
      feel in no danger of losing dignity when they adapt themselves to
      incomprehensible humbugs.

In those pleasant little towns on Thames, you may hear the fall of the
      water over the weirs, or even, in still weather, the rustle of the rushes;

      child, playfully gliding away among the trees, unpolluted by the
      defilements that lie in wait for it on its course, and as yet out of
      hearing of the deep summons of the sea. It were too much to pretend that
      Betty Higden made out such thoughts; no; but she heard the tender river
      whispering to many like herself, ‘Come to me, come to me! When the cruel
      shame and terror you have so long fled from, most beset you, come to me! I
      am the Relieving Officer appointed by eternal ordinance to do my work; I
      am not held in estimation according as I shirk it. My breast is softer
      than the pauper-nurse’s; death in my arms is peacefuller than among the
      pauper-wards. Come to me!’
